title: Financial modelling, Lesson 2: Forecasting revenue from real drivers
subtitle: Why 'grows 10% a year' is a lazy assumption
whyItMatters: Revenue is the first line and the line that governs the whole model - get it wrong and everything below it is wrong too. Forecasting from real drivers instead of a generic growth rate is the single biggest difference between a model that persuades and a model that gets thrown out.
openingQuestion: Which way of forecasting revenue is most persuasive when you present it to an investor?
openingOptions: Assume revenue grows a steady 10% a year for five years
Split it into testable drivers: volume × price
Take the industry average growth and apply it to the company
Use the growth rate the company posted in its latest year
explanation: A driver-based forecast breaks revenue into components that can each be challenged and tested on their own. Instead of arguing about whether 10% is reasonable - a question nobody can settle - you argue about each variable: is there enough capacity, can prices actually be raised, where is the market share coming from. That is a discussion with evidence in it.

realWorldExample.description: For a chain of stores, forecasting 'revenue up 15%' has almost no analytical content. The right way is to split it: closing store count × average revenue per store, where store count itself splits into existing stores plus openings minus closures. Now an investor can challenge each assumption on its own: is a plan to open 20 stores feasible in terms of capital and available sites?

quiz.question: What does driver-based forecasting mean?
options: Splitting revenue into variables that can be tested
Applying one fixed growth rate to every forecast year
Using only historical figures to extrapolate later years
Taking the forecast straight from a broker's research report
quiz.explanation: The substance of it is decomposing revenue into components that mean something commercially, so each assumption can be discussed against evidence. A single fixed rate cannot be tested, pure extrapolation assumes the past mechanism still holds without saying what that mechanism is, and lifting a broker's number simply moves the same unexamined assumption into your model under someone else's name.

quiz.question: For a SaaS business, what is the most sensible way to decompose revenue?
options: Total marketing spend multiplied by a conversion factor
Opening customers + new customers − churn, times ARPU
Sales headcount multiplied by their average productivity
Market capitalisation multiplied by expected growth
quiz.explanation: A SaaS model revolves around a recurring customer base: you need to track new customers, the churn rate, and average revenue per user (ARPU). Marketing spend and sales headcount are inputs that feed the new-customer line rather than the whole of revenue, and neither of them says anything about churn. Market capitalisation is an output of the market's view of the company - using it to forecast revenue reasons in a circle.

quiz.question: Why should a revenue forecast be checked against a capacity constraint?
options: Because plant capacity sets the annual tax bill
Because the auditor requires this check to be performed
Because the model can produce output beyond capacity
Because designed capacity always equals maximum revenue
quiz.explanation: Excel does not know the plant can only make one million units a year. Without a constraint you impose yourself, the model will cheerfully forecast three million units and raise no error. Capacity has nothing to do with the tax bill, and an auditor does not review internal models at all. Nor does designed capacity equal maximum revenue - price and product mix sit between the two.

quiz.question: Which sign suggests a revenue forecast is not credible?
options: Revenue is broken out by individual product line
Growth differs between the years of the forecast period
It comes with a base, upside and downside scenario analysis
One flat growth number for five years, tied to no driver
quiz.explanation: Growth that is perfectly flat and cannot be explained is the classic marker of a lazy assumption - usually rejected the moment somebody asks where the number came from. The other three are all signs of care: a product-line breakout, growth that varies as the business's own circumstances vary, and an explicit set of scenarios each make the forecast easier to challenge, which is the point.

quiz.question: Why is a revenue forecast built from a single growth rate so hard to argue with?
options: Because nobody can point to where the number is wrong to fix it
Because growth rates shift every year and cannot be held fixed
Because it ignores how inflation feeds through to selling prices
Because you need three years of history to compute the rate
quiz.explanation: An argument about a ten percent number ends with whoever feels more reasonable. Split it into volume times price and each side can be tested against plant capacity, signed contracts or the industry price level. Inflation is one input among many rather than the core defect, growth rates varying is a reason to model drivers rather than a barrier, and three years of history is not required to compute a rate at all.

keyTakeaways: Split revenue into drivers: volume × price, or customers × value × frequency
Every driver must be testable against data or against a specific plan
Always check against real constraints: capacity, market size, available resource
One flat growth number held for years on end is the mark of a lazy assumption

practicePrompt.question: A plant has maximum capacity of 1 million units a year and currently runs 800,000. The model forecasts volume growing 15% a year for five years. What is the problem?
options: No problem here, 15% is a reasonable growth rate
By year 2, output already exceeds design capacity
It should be lowered to 10% to be safe
Switch to forecasting revenue rather than volume
practicePrompt.explanation: 800,000 × 1.15 = 920,000 (still within capacity); × 1.15 again = 1,058,000, over the 1 million ceiling. From year 3 onward the model is forecasting something physically impossible. The right fix: either add a capacity expansion CapEx assumption with the costs that go with it, or cap the line with a MIN function at the ceiling.

summary.keyIdea: Revenue is the product of testable drivers, not a growth rate imposed from outside
summary.commonMistake: Using one blanket growth rate for every year without tying it to any commercial driver.
summary.action: Pick a business and try decomposing its revenue into 2-3 principal drivers.

application.title: Decompose a real company's revenue
application.message: Take the annual report of a listed company. Find which drivers they disclose: store count, volume, subscriber numbers, average selling price. Try rebuilding the latest year's revenue from those drivers.
application.secondary: If it reconciles to the reported revenue, you have understood their business model correctly.

sections.text: Revenue is the first line of the model and it governs everything below. It is also where the modeller is most tempted to be lazy: type one growth number and drag it right across five years.

A growth rate imposed from outside cannot be challenged. Your audience can only say 'that feels a bit high' or 'sounds fair enough' - there is no basis for a discussion. Split revenue into volume and price, by contrast, and each part attaches to a question that data can answer.

left.label: An imposed assumption
left.text: Revenue = last year × 110%. Nobody knows where the 10% came from, and there is no way to test it.

right.label: A driver-based forecast
right.text: Revenue = volume × price, where volume is tied to capacity and price is tied to the market level. Each variable can be tested on its own.

sections.text: Ways to decompose by business type

items: **Manufacturing:** volume × average selling price, constrained by plant capacity
**Retail:** number of outlets × average revenue per outlet; outlet count = opening + openings − closures
**SaaS / subscription:** opening customers + new − churned, times average revenue per customer
**Services:** billable headcount × billable hours × hourly rate

sections.label: Excel does not know about physical limits
sections.text: The model will happily forecast volume above plant capacity, market share above 100%, or a customer count larger than the population. Real-world constraints have to be put in by you - there is no automatic warning.

lines: A good forecast is not one that predicts correctly, but one that makes clear what you are betting on.
Next lesson: linking the three statements - the heart of a financial model.
